podcast.title: "Lush" Sound
podcast.body: The music associated with Philadelphia International Records and Philly Soul is frequently described as "lush" in various writings, with its characteristic string instruments creating an enveloping, wave-like sonic experience that naturally encourages physical movement. "The word that comes up so often in articles and books and essays about Gamble and Huff is lush."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Blending Motown and Stax
podcast.body: Mark Neal, a professor of African American Studies at Duke, characterized Gamble and Huff's unique achievement in Philly Soul as successfully melding "the Motown machine with the Stacks grit," resulting in a sound that is simultaneously glossy and smooth yet possesses the raw intensity associated with Stax Records. "Mark Neal, professor of African American Studies at Duke said of Gamble and Huff, quote, they found a way to marry the Motown machine with the Stacks grit."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Distinctive Sound Description
podcast.body: Journalist Jim Farber (2021) vividly described Philly Soul as "a mixture of creamy strings, punching horns, snaking bass lines and fullsome melodies all combined to create something at once complex and light, a sonic suple fired by soul." Producer and guitarist Bobby Eli famously encapsulated the sound as "funk, dressed in a tuxedo." "He wrote, it is a mixture of creamy strings, punching horns, snaking bass lines and fullsome melodies all combined to create something at once complex and light, a sonic suple fired by soul."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Integration of Social Commentary
podcast.body: Beyond its appealing and sweet sonic qualities, Gamble and Huff's Philly Soul consciously integrated social commentary, reflecting their attentiveness to contemporary world events and their intention to use music as a medium for conveying deeper, meaningful messages. "There's something more underneath that sweetness, but Gamble and Huff made no pretenses that they didn't pay attention to what was happening in the world."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Producer's Genre
podcast.body: Philly Soul is characterized as a "producer's genre," underscoring the significant influence of producers like Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff in shaping its signature sound and intricate arrangements, a characteristic that also served as a precursor to the rise of Disco. "Philly's soul is a bit of a producer's genre, also foreshadowing Disco by the way"

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Racial Integration ("Gray Eyed")
podcast.body: In 1978, Billy Paul described Philadelphia soul as "gray eyed," signifying its inherent and enduring racial integration in both its appeal and composition, thereby challenging racial stereotypes often associated with "black music." "Paul said in 1978 that at that all Philadelphia soul is what he called gray eyed meaning racially integrated and it always has been."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Signature Element: Strings
podcast.body: The prominent and "creamy" use of string arrangements is identified as the hallmark of Philly Soul, providing its distinctive and enveloping sound that sets it apart from other soul genres, such as Motown. "Of course, the element that's missing that makes Philly soul, Philly soul are the strings."
